"""A local spelling detector around L, U and V.

Short U-initial continuations after L are positive, with larger responses
for UN/UP and POLU/POLY spellings (especially Cyrillic POLU). LV, Latin VV and
V-UL spellings are negative; VALV stems and CJK valve words more strongly
so. Split UTF-8 fragments of gate-radical characters are negative too.
Other text is near zero. These are local spelling approximations, not a
claim that all these fragments have one shared meaning.
"""
from anyascii import anyascii
import unihan

READS = ()
GATE_RADICAL = 169  # Kangxi radical: gate / door


def local_value(previous, token):
    word = token.strip().lower()
    a = anyascii(previous).lower()
    b = anyascii(token).lower()
    joined = a + b
    if 'valv' in b:
        return -11.0
    if ('valv' not in a and 'valv' in joined
            and not token.startswith(' ')):
        return -9.0
    if word in {'阀', '閥'}:
        return -10.0
    if word == '弁':
        return -2.0
    if 'lv' in b and len(b) <= 4 and not b.startswith(' '):
        return -2.5
    if a.endswith('v') and len(b) <= 4:
        if b.startswith('ul') or token.startswith(('v', 'V')):
            return -2.5
    if not a.endswith('l'):
        return 0.0
    if b.startswith('v') and len(b) <= 3:
        return -1.4
    if (previous.lower().endswith('пол') and token.startswith('у')
            and len(token) <= 2):
        return 10.0
    if a.endswith('pol') and token.startswith(('u', 'y')) and len(b) <= 3:
        return 3.5
    if not b.startswith('u'):
        return 0.0
    if (previous.lower().endswith('л') and token.startswith('у')
            and len(token) <= 2):
        return 1.8
    if ((token == 'un' or token.startswith('up') and len(token) <= 3)
            and len(a.strip()) > 1 and not a.endswith('ll')):
        return 5.5
    if b.startswith(('uj', 'uz')) and len(b) <= 4:
        return 2.5
    if len(b) <= 3:
        return 0.5
    return 0.0


def gate_fragment(previous_bytes, token_bytes):
    """Recognize a gate radical even while its UTF-8 character is split."""
    raw = previous_bytes + token_bytes
    tail = raw[-2:]
    if (len(tail) == 2 and 0xE0 <= tail[0] < 0xF0
            and 0x80 <= tail[1] < 0xC0):
        first_completion = (tail + b'\x80').decode('utf-8', 'ignore')
        if (len(first_completion) == 1
                and unihan.radical(first_completion) == GATE_RADICAL):
            return -6.0
    if token_bytes and token_bytes[0] & 0xC0 == 0x80:
        text = raw.decode('utf-8', 'ignore')
        if text and unihan.radical(text[-1]) == GATE_RADICAL:
            return -4.0
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    document = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    previous = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == document else ''
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    raw = prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    old_raw = carry[2] if carry is not None and carry[0] == document else b''
    value = gate_fragment(old_raw, raw) or local_value(previous, token)
    return (document, token, raw), value

"""Recognize a few recurring textual completions.

The main response is to periods after scholarly abbreviations: Fig., pp.,
e.g., i.e., and related reference labels. Additional positive responses mark
Java final declarations, PDF references, and opening LaTeX math environments.
There is a small negative default at document starts; otherwise the default
is zero. A short text suffix is reset at each document boundary.
"""
import re

READS = ()

# Conventional printed cross-references and scholarly abbreviations.
ABBREVIATIONS = {
    'Fig': 3.5, 'fig': 1.6, 'FIG': 0.85,
    'Figs': 2.4, 'figs': 2.0, 'FIGS': 0.8,
    'p': 1.2, 'pp': 3.0,
    'Eq': 1.65, 'Eqs': 2.4, 'eq': 1.4,
    'No': 1.1, 'Nos': 1.7, 'no': 0.2,
    'Vol': 3.4, 'vol': 2.0,
    'Ref': 2.9, 'ref': 1.7, 'Sect': 2.7,
    'Sec': 1.1, 'App': 1.8, 'Pat': 0.8,
    'Ser': 0.7, 'Prop': 0.8, 'Ex': 0.8,
    'cf': 1.3, 'Cf': 0.8, 'al': 0.4,
    'etc': 0.25, 'vs': 0.3, 'v': 0.2,
    'Cir': 0.55, 'Prof': 0.8,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    tail = '' if carry is None or carry[0] != doc else carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = -0.25 if not tail else 0.0
    if token == '.':
        match = re.search(r'([A-Za-z]+)$', tail)
        if match:
            value = ABBREVIATIONS.get(match[1], 0.0)
        if re.search(r'\be\.g$', tail):
            value = 3.55
        elif re.search(r'\bi\.e$', tail):
            value = 3.3
    elif token.strip() == 'final':
        if re.search(r'\b(?:private|public|protected)\s*$', tail):
            value = 4.3
        elif re.search(r'\bstatic\s*$', tail):
            value = 1.7
        elif re.search(r'(?:\n|\\n)[ \t]*$', tail):
            value = 0.6
    elif token == '}' and re.search(
        r'\\begin\{(?:align\*?|aligned|[pb]?matrix|cases)$', tail
    ):

    elif token.strip() == 'PDF':
        value = 1.2
        if re.search(r'\bDownload$', tail):
            value = 7.0
        elif re.search(r'\bGet$', tail):
            value = 4.0
    elif token.strip() == 'pdf':
        value = 0.4
    return (doc, (tail + token)[-96:]), value

"""A full stop that closes a reference abbreviation, such as the "." in "Fig. 3",
"e.g. [2]", "i.e. the", "No. 5" or "p. 12".

What it responds to: the model expects a label or number right after these abbreviations,
and the full stop is where it starts to predict one. Mixed-case "Fig." and "e.g."/"i.e."
give the strongest responses. The all-caps patent style "FIG." and "p."/"No." are weaker.
Ordinary sentence full stops stay at 0.

It also gives a small negative value on the first token of each document (the token right
after <|endoftext|>, or the first token of a row), which is the other consistent feature.

Everything else predicts 0. Most of the component's variance is diffuse small noise that
no short rule captures.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Abbreviation just before the full stop, after a space, bracket or punctuation.
ABBREV = re.compile(r"(?:^|[\s(\[,;])(e\.g|i\.e|Fig|Figs|FIG|FIGS|Vol|Eq|Ref|Sec|No|Nos|p|pp|Pat|App|Ser|cf)\.$")

# Typical activation after each abbreviation's full stop, from training text.
STRENGTH = {
    "e.g": 3.5, "i.e": 3.5, "Fig": 3.4, "Figs": 2.9, "Vol": 3.5,
    "FIG": 1.0, "FIGS": 2.0, "No": 1.3, "Nos": 2.0, "p": 1.0, "pp": 1.5,
    "Eq": 2.0, "Ref": 2.0, "Sec": 1.5, "Pat": 1.0, "App": 1.0, "Ser": 1.0, "cf": 1.5,
}

FIRST_TOKEN_OF_DOCUMENT = -0.27


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    if len(tokens) == 1 or docs[-1] != docs[-2]:
        return None, FIRST_TOKEN_OF_DOCUMENT
    if tokens[-1] != ".":
        return None, 0.0
    match = ABBREV.search("".join(tokens[-4:]))
    if match is None:
        return None, 0.0
    return None, STRENGTH[match.group(1)]

"""Mid-line indentation: whitespace that indents code but does not follow a real newline.

In ordinary code the indent after a newline is ignored by this component. It responds to
indentation that sits mid-line, after something that is not a newline:
  * a line number in a numbered listing, as in "583<TAB>{", or
  * a literal backslash-n escape, as in code quoted inside a JSON string ("\\n    ").
There, a tab (at any length) or a run of two or more spaces is strongly negative. Other
mid-line indentation is weakly negative. Everything else is near zero.
"""

READS = ()

STRONG = -1.5   # indentation right after a line number or a literal "\n"
WEAK = -0.3     # indentation anywhere else mid-line
BLANKS = " \t\xa0"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else "\n"
    indent = tok != "" and tok.strip(BLANKS) == "" and ("\t" in tok or len(tok) >= 2)
    if not indent or "\n" in prev:
        return carry, 0.0
    if prev.isdigit() or prev == "n":
        return carry, STRONG
    return carry, WEAK

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:765 -- a few readable triggers in the text.

Positive (the year rule dominates):
1. DECADE DIGIT OF A YEAR. Fires on the third digit of a four-digit year that
   starts with "19" or "20" (the "8" in 1988, the "1" in 2015). It grows with the
   decade: about 0 for 190x, about 0.5 for 195x, about 0.9 for 198x/199x, about 1.0
   for 201x, and 0.55 to 0.7 for 200x and 202x. The last digit of a year is ~0.
2. NUMBER AS THE FIRST TOKEN OF A TEXT. A digit 4 to 8 that is the very first token
   of a document gives a strong positive value (about 1.2).

Negative (indentation that is not at the start of a real line):
3. TAB AFTER A LINE NUMBER. In a numbered code listing ("   261<TAB>    code"), the
   tab (with or without indent spaces) that separates the line number from the code
   is strongly negative, about -0.9.
4. INDENT AFTER AN ESCAPED NEWLINE. Indentation spaces that follow a literal
   backslash-n (two characters, as in code pasted inside a JSON string) are
   negative, about -0.7. Indentation after a real newline stays near zero.

Everything else predicts 0.
"""

READS = ()

# Decade digit (third digit of the year) -> activation, for years starting 19 or 20.
YEAR_DECADE = {
    "190": 0.0, "191": 0.05, "192": 0.1, "193": 0.25, "194": 0.4,
    "195": 0.5, "196": 0.6, "197": 0.8, "198": 0.85, "199": 0.9,
    "200": 0.55, "201": 0.95, "202": 0.7,
}
TAB_AFTER_LINE_NUMBER = -0.9
INDENT_AFTER_ESCAPED_NEWLINE = -0.7
FIRST_TOKEN_DIGIT = 1.2  # digits 4-8 only


def _is_digit_token(s):
    return len(s) > 0 and s.isdigit()


def _is_whitespace_token(s):
    return len(s) > 0 and s.strip(" \t") == ""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    cur = prefix.token_strings[t]
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    strings = prefix.token_strings
    # k: position within the current document (0 at a document's first token).
    k = 0 if t == 0 or docs[t - 1] != docs[t] else carry + 1

    value = 0.0
    # Rule 1: third digit of a year that starts 19 or 20.
    if len(cur) == 1 and cur.isdigit() and k >= 2:
        pre = strings[t - 2] + strings[t - 1]
        if pre in ("19", "20"):
            value = YEAR_DECADE.get(pre + cur, 0.0)
    # Rule 2: a digit 4-8 as the very first token of a document.
    if k == 0 and cur in ("4", "5", "6", "7", "8"):
        value = FIRST_TOKEN_DIGIT
    # Rule 3: tab-indent right after a line number.
    if k >= 1 and "\t" in cur and _is_whitespace_token(cur) and _is_digit_token(strings[t - 1]):
        value = TAB_AFTER_LINE_NUMBER
    # Rule 4: indentation right after a literal backslash-n.
    if k >= 2 and _is_whitespace_token(cur) and "\t" not in cur:
        before = strings[t - 2] + strings[t - 1]
        if before.endswith("\\n"):
            value = INDENT_AFTER_ESCAPED_NEWLINE
    return k, float(value)

"""layers.1.mlp.down_proj:766 - an "English verb COME" detector (negative), with a few
look-alike spellings and a couple of small positive side-cases.

What the component does, in plain terms:
  * It switches strongly negative on the word "come" in its inflected forms
    (come, comes, came, coming), as it is written as a whole word in English text.
    "come true", "come back", "come from" give the largest negative values (-4 to -9).
    Italian "come" (= "as/how") gives roughly nothing, and so do "become", "income",
    "welcome", "outcome", "overcome" (the letters "come" inside a longer word do not count).
  * It is moderately negative on words that look like "come" spelled differently:
    cum, cream, corn, cone, cane, cam (and their capitalised forms).
  * It is weakly positive on the word "going" and on the capital codes CE, CS, CG, CF.
  * It is weakly negative on runs of middle dots (the token "··").
  * Everything else is about zero.

The program tracks the word being spelled out (the letters since the last non-letter
character), so a word split across several tokens is still recognised.  The word is
reset at each new document.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Activation values for whole words (lower-cased), from the training data.
WORD_VALUES = {
    "come": -4.0,
    "comes": -4.0,
    "came": -2.8,
    "coming": -3.0,
    "cum": -2.5,
    "cream": -2.5,
    "corn": -2.5,
    "corns": -2.5,
    "cone": -2.5,
    "cones": -2.5,
    "cane": -2.5,
    "canes": -2.5,
    "cam": -2.5,
    "cams": -2.5,
    "cumin": -2.5,
    "going": 0.45,
}
# Exact (case-sensitive) token strings, for capital codes and dot runs.
TOKEN_VALUES = {"CE": 0.6, "CS": 0.6, "CG": 0.6, "CF": 0.6, "··": -1.1}

TRAILING_LETTERS = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z]*$")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document id, letters of the word being spelled so far), or None at a row start.
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        word = ""
    else:
        word = carry[1]

    piece = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    tail = TRAILING_LETTERS.search(piece).group(0)
    # A piece made only of letters continues the word; anything else starts a new one.
    word = word + piece.lower() if tail == piece else tail.lower()

    if piece in TOKEN_VALUES:
        value = TOKEN_VALUES[piece]
    else:
        value = WORD_VALUES.get(word, 0.0)
    return (doc, word), float(value)

"""Predicts layers.1.mlp.down_proj:767 from document position and the first token's kind.

This component is nearly silent: its activation has std 0.03 almost everywhere and
never passes the causal-importance threshold in a 10M-token corpus. Its one consistent
signal is on the first token of each document (the token right after <|endoftext|>, or
the first token of a row). There the activation is usually negative, and how negative
depends on what kind of token it is. At that position attention sees only the token
itself, so this is the token's own embedding speaking, not any context.
Everywhere else the activation has no simple pattern (no token class, previous token
class or depth in the document moves its mean), so the program predicts 0 there.
"""

READS = ()

# Mean activation on a document's first token, by the token's kind (training rows).
FIRST_TOKEN_VALUE = {
    "word": -0.10,  # plain Latin letters, with or without a leading space
    "non_latin": 0.02,  # CJK and other non-ASCII scripts
    "blank_or_mixed": -0.22,  # whitespace only, or letters mixed with digits/symbols
    "other": -0.09,  # punctuation, digits, and the rest
}


def kind(text):
    body = text.strip()
    if "�" in text or text.startswith("<|"):
        return "other"
    if body == "":
        return "blank_or_mixed"
    if not body.isascii():
        return "non_latin"
    if body.isalpha():
        return "word"
    if any(ch.isalpha() for ch in body):
        return "blank_or_mixed"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    starts_doc = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    if not starts_doc:
        return None, 0.0
    return None, FIRST_TOKEN_VALUE[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]
